attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, given as his own view, not a quote of Chomsky.

semantics.note: Keeps 'certainly', 'anything whatsoever', the 'why ... rather than some other way' scope, and the 'ditto' for the mind. It is a firm retrospective statement.

contract.note: The plain reading is mostly fair, but the result depends on whether model-based evidence about mechanisms counts as explaining 'why ... rather than some other way'. Marcus never defined that bar, and the contract admits it is contested.

evidence.note: Peer-reviewed PNAS paper (Nov 2021), before the post. It says transformer models give evidence that predictive processing shapes human language comprehension. That is relevant to the mind, but whether it meets the undefined 'why rather than otherwise' bar is contested, so it does not decide the claim.

reviews.rationale: There is one relevant item: a peer-reviewed claim that LLM-brain modelling shows how predictive processing shapes language comprehension. It cuts against 'anything whatsoever' only if mechanistic evidence counts as teaching us why the mind is as it is rather than otherwise. Marcus did not define that standard and it is philosophically contested. The packet also does not review the wider literature. The evidence does not settle the claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own judgement of his counting and sorting example, rebutting Sejnowski's quoted remark.

semantics.note: Correctly limited to the one prompt and response he showed. It is a firm observation about that exchange.

contract.note: Checking the actual prompt for clarity and the response for errors is a fair, ordinary test of what he said.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no evidence items. The prompt and response (likely an image in the post) were not recovered, so neither the prompt's clarity nor the alleged counting or sorting errors can be checked independently. Marcus's own assertion cannot prove itself. The case is not broken; the evidence is simply missing.

attribution.note: Marcus's own general statement about LLM generalization in his post.

semantics.note: Keeps the 'essentially everything' and 'nearly any' scope and 'can be easily broken'. It is a firm, near-universal description of what LLMs could do at the time.

contract.note: The plain reading (small or moderate input changes break generalization across most domains) is ordinary. But 'easily broken' has no threshold and the scope is near-universal, so the result depends on how much evidence across domains is required.

evidence.note: Shi et al. (v1, Jan 2023): adding irrelevant context sharply cuts LLM math accuracy. This shows brittleness under a small change, but only for grade-school math, and the authors report ways to reduce it.

Razeghi et al. (Feb 2022): numerical reasoning accuracy depends on how often terms appear in pretraining data. This fits generalization limited to similar examples, but only in numerical tasks on Pile-trained GPT models.

Minerva paper (Jun 2022): over 80% accuracy on 10-digit addition, so in this case generalization to rare inputs did not break easily. It is a single counterexample in one domain, not a broad refutation.

reviews.rationale: The evidence covers only arithmetic and math reasoning. Two studies show brittleness under small shifts, and one shows fairly robust long-addition generalization. None tests the near-universal 'essentially everything' scope across domains, and 'easily broken' has no agreed threshold. The packet cannot show that nearly any generalization breaks, or that it doesn't.
